prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, opening the 10^-18 regime of atomic timekeeping

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B035 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. After the full first round the case has, if anything, become more precise, because the chair's first question has an answer that can be written into the citation. The physical step that separates lattice clocks from the 2005 and 2012 work is that Katori's magic-wavelength condition makes the light shift of the clock transition cancel while a large ensemble of neutral atoms is held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so that Doppler and recoil effects are suppressed and the statistical power of many atoms is obtained at once. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as the tool that counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems; neither covers interrogating a many-atom lattice with the trapping potential itself made invisible to the transition. Ye's group then showed that the many-body and systematic effects could be controlled down to the 10^-18 level, and that level has been reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, which is a stricter independent test than most prize-worthy results have faced. The consequences (constancy of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy, dark-matter searches, the open discussion on redefining the second) are real. I would draft the citation around the invention and its realization, and carry the 10^-18 regime as the demonstrated consequence and not as the claim itself. For a single prize part with two names this is the cleanest configuration on the shortlist, and I would add no second part.
statement.case_against: The reservations I recorded in round 1 are not removed, only bounded. The first is overlap: every B035 supporter lists the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and a citation phrased as 'better clocks' would read as a sequel to them. The second is that Lemonde, Takamoto and the Sr and Yb groups at SYRTE, PTB, NIST and elsewhere, and the ion-clock community, are outside a two-name prize, so the committee should state openly that the two names stand for the decisive concept and its leading realization and not for the whole field. The third is timing: the redefinition of the second has not been decided, and a committee that wanted to wait for that decision would not be unreasonable, although I do not think the scientific case depends on it. Finally, B035 is a precision-measurement achievement, and Mehlig and Danielsson are right that B008 or the Higgs discovery could be argued to be conceptually larger; I accept that, and do not think a clean credit should outweigh science, only that here the science is strong enough that the clean credit is a tiebreaker in its favour and not a substitute for it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B008 on the grounds that it combines a new organizing principle (Z2 topology), a rapid decisive experiment in HgTe and field-wide consequences, but says he would not defend it against a well-argued shift to B035 because of the credit problem.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing configuration and I take it seriously. In round 1 I asked whether the committee could say what is new in the lattice clock; having now read your statement and Mehlig's, I think the answer is the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice, and I would ask you to test that against the citation I propose. I agree with you that B008 is the larger idea. Where I stay on B035 is that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, with Zhang deceased and the three-dimensional work outside the names, mean a three-name B008 cannot describe the historical sequence, whereas the clock pair can. I am not persuaded by the 2016 overlap argument as a bar to B008 on its own, but together with the attribution gap it keeps B008 as my first alternative and not my choice.

responses.point: Mehlig now places B035 first but warns that a citation written around 'better clocks' will read as a sequel to 2005 and 2012, and that a clean attribution should not count for more than the science.
responses.response: I agree with both cautions and have tried to meet the first in the citation wording: it names the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice as the invention and the 10^-18 regime as the consequence. I also accept your second point; in my own reasoning the unanimous Katori-Ye proposal is information about how well the history maps onto two names, not a measure of merit, and I have not used it as one. I would add one qualification to your doubt on widening the list: I agree it would break the three-name limit and dilute the citation, but the committee should record that Lemonde, Takamoto and the Sr and Yb groups are outside the credit, so that the narrow citation is a deliberate statement and not an oversight.

responses.point: Pearce proposes a two-part configuration, B035 with Katori and Ye plus B023 with Halzen alone, and flags that credit to one name leaves Karle and Spiering out.
responses.response: I accept the instrument-builder argument and that the diffuse high-energy flux is established, and I agree that the committee should not add a part merely because it touches a member's field, as you say yourself. My difficulty is the one you name: a one-name credit for IceCube after the Katori-Ye pair is an attribution compromise that the supplied record does not let me defend, and the case against the second part is stated in Danielsson's and Lindroth's responses as well (unresolved origin of most of the flux, incomplete water-based confirmation). I would therefore keep B035 as a single part and treat IceCube as a candidate for a later year when source identification is firmer and the credit can be given in a way the committee can defend. B023 is not on my alternatives list for this reason, not because I doubt the discovery.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B035 from B006 and still weighs the Higgs discovery higher in pure scientific significance, while holding that the three-name limit makes the ATLAS and CMS credit arbitrary.
responses.response: I agree that the importance of the Higgs discovery is not in doubt and that I cannot see a principled three-name rule for it from the supplied material, which is why I do not put B006 in my configuration. I would correct one point in how you describe my position: I ranked the lattice clock first at the opening and did not move toward it, so the effect of your argument on me was to sharpen the citation, not to change the ranking. On your remaining question, I think your own physical argument, that a clock resolving gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample is a new measurement regime, is the best evidence that lattice clocks are distinct from single-ion clocks, and I would use it in the committee's justification.

responses.point: Johansson has moved to B035 and notes that Ye's contribution is a sustained programme of systematic-uncertainty reduction and many-body clock physics, and that the case would be stronger if the second were already redefined.
responses.response: On your first point I agree and this is why the citation should name the lattice-clock invention and its realization and not precision spectroscopy broadly; a broad wording would drift back toward the 2005 prize. On timing I remain slightly more cautious than Lindroth, Mehlig and Pearce, who treat the redefinition as supporting: it would strengthen the case, but I do not think the scientific merit changes if the decision comes later. I note your own disclosure on circuit QED and share your reasoning that a second superconducting-circuit prize close to 2025 is a cost; I keep B004 as an alternative because it is original and mature, with the 2025 overlap and the missing Girvin credit as the open points.

responses.point: Lindroth agrees on the lattice-clock architecture and its 10^-18 systematics as the core, and argues that the field is mature and that recognition is neither premature nor a lifetime award.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the qualitative difference from single-ion clocks, since the many-atom interrogation is what the lattice provides. I disagree mildly with your point that the comb prize recognised only a tool: the clock does rest on the comb, and that is precisely why the citation must not claim the comb, and I would rather the committee state that explicitly than rely on the reader to draw the line. The Sr versus Yb and SYRTE contributions are still a fair point that the two-name list is not uncontested, and I would record that, as you suggest, as an acknowledged uncertainty and not as a reason to change the names.

uncertainties: Whether the credited names Katori and Ye adequately reflect the clock community, given Lemonde, Takamoto, the PTB and SYRTE groups and the Yb-clock work, which a two-name prize cannot express.

Whether the committee accepts the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the citation wording can carry that distinction.
How much the undecided redefinition of the second should matter; I treat it as supporting and not necessary, but that is a judgement and others reasonably differ.
I rely on my own recollection of the clock timeline, accuracy records and priority and have not verified details from the nomination files, which I am not permitted to read at this stage.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I spent time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is part of the frequency-comb background of the JILA environment in which Jun Ye works; I know of no documented personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye themselves, and I do not consider it grounds for recusal from B035, but the committee should have it on record since the comb prize is the main precedent we are weighing. I am a Lund atomic physicist with a quantum-memory and WACQT background, which touches B004 and B015, neither of which is in my configuration; my Lund colleagues Rippe, Walther and Kinos are not nominated. I have no tie to B008, B023 or the other shortlisted parts.
